studies.meaning: A promise made to people who left. The clause specifying that they emigrated for God's sake after being wronged sets two conditions at once, a motive and a prior injury, and the commentators treat both as load-bearing. What is promised is a settling, in this world, in something good, and then a larger reward afterwards. The sentence closes with a conditional half-line that is left hanging: if only they knew. The subject of that clause is disputed among the commentators.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is Meccan, but many classical commentators hold this ayah and the one after it to belong to a later stage. Some read them of the migration to Abyssinia during the Meccan years, when a group left to escape persecution; others hold them to be among the Medinan ayat of this surah and read them of the emigration to Medina. The reports differ, and the tradition preserves both readings side by side rather than settling on one.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to cut off or abandon, so the word carries severance rather than travel. It names leaving people and a place behind, which is why it also gives the word for parting speech.
A verb for assigning someone a dwelling and putting them in it, doubled here with emphatic markers. The word implies being housed by another's arrangement rather than finding a place yourself.
Deliberately unspecified. Commentators list safety, provision, honour and victory among the readings, and note that leaving the noun open lets the promise fit whatever the emigrant actually lacked.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving your tribe was close to unthinkable. Protection came from kin, and a man outside that network had no one to avenge him, no one to stand surety for a debt, and no claim on hospitality beyond the customary three days. Emigrants arrived somewhere as dependants with no standing at all. The word this ayah uses for settling them is the word for being given a place by someone else, which is exactly the position such people were in.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase used here, emigrating for God's sake, occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Other passages speak of emigrating in God's way or for His cause, using a different preposition. Classical commentators note the difference, reading this construction as naming God as the whole object of the move rather than the direction of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The promise is deliberately double, and the order matters: something good here first, and only then the greater reward. That refuses a purely deferred consolation, which would have been the easier thing to offer people who had lost houses and trade. The trailing clause about knowledge then does something quieter. It suggests the difficulty of the situation is not only material but epistemic, since what would make the loss bearable is information the sufferer does not yet have.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same promise to those who emigrated and were then killed or died on the way.
Describes the earth as containing many a refuge and abundance for one who emigrates.
Tells believing servants that God's earth is spacious, so worship Him wherever you are.

studies.applyIt: If you have moved away from somewhere, for whatever reason, name one good thing that came from the move that you could not have arranged yourself. Not to balance the ledger, and not instead of what was lost. This ayah puts the worldly good first and does not pretend it settles anything. Naming it accurately is different from being consoled by it.

studies.title: Ask Those Who Know
studies.meaning: The first line finishes the previous sentence by naming what those emigrants did: they held out, and they relied on their Lord. The two are given in that order, endurance first and reliance second, which the commentators read as describing a sequence rather than two names for one thing. The second line turns to an objection about the messenger being an ordinary man, and answers it by pointing outward: put the question to people who have the relevant knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is Meccan, though a number of classical commentators hold the preceding ayat about emigration to belong to a later stage. The objection answered in the second line was a live Meccan complaint, that a genuine messenger would be an angel rather than a man from a known family. The people directed to are generally understood as those familiar with earlier scriptures, who could confirm that every previous messenger had also been human.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to confine or restrain. The word is closer to holding a position than to accepting a fate, which is why it also gives the word for binding an animal in one place.
From the root for appointing an agent to act on your behalf. The grammar implies handing a matter over after doing your part, not instead of doing it, which is how the commentators read it.

Covers remembrance, mention and a revealed book. Attached to people it names those who carry the earlier revelations in memory, which is why the phrase is usually read as a direction to prior scripture.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had Jewish and Christian communities within reach, in Yathrib, in Yemen and along the northern trade roads, and Meccan merchants dealt with them regularly. Monks and rabbis were consulted as a matter of course on questions about earlier prophets, and stories from those scriptures circulated in Arabic by word of mouth. Directing an objector to ask them was practical advice, not a rhetorical gesture. The people meant could be found on the next journey north.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to ask the people of the reminder occurs in exactly two places in the Quran, here and in surah 21, and the two ayat are nearly identical: both begin by saying that only men were sent before, both add that they received revelation, and both close with the same conditional about not knowing. The pairing is one of the closest verbal repetitions between two surahs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Answering a theological objection by directing people to inquire is unusual, and the commentators note what it assumes: that the record of earlier prophecy is public, checkable, and consistent with the claim being made. It treats revelation as continuous rather than unprecedented. The two words in the first line establish something separate, that reliance on God is compatible with strain, since patience is named as the thing being done while the reliance is going on.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction in nearly identical words and adds that those sent ate food.
Answers the same objection by noting that every messenger before ate and walked in markets.
Sets out what reliance on God is promised to produce, a way out and provision unlooked for.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have an opinion about but have never asked anyone qualified. Find a person who actually knows and ask them a single question, phrased so it can be answered. This ayah answers a serious objection by telling the objector where to look, which assumes the asking is available. Usually it still is, and we simply do not do it.

studies.title: The Cry And The Forgetting
studies.meaning: A sequence rather than a rule. Every blessing is traced to one source; then harm arrives and people call out to that source with a word that means bellowing, not praying; then the harm lifts and a portion of them attach partners to their Lord again. The commentators note the careful limiting word, a portion, which keeps the description from becoming a charge against everyone. The closing line is left ominously short.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just stated that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God and asked why anyone would fear another. This passage answers by describing behaviour rather than argument. Mecca depended on trade routes that ran through drought, raiding and storm at sea, so the experience being described was common: vows made in danger and quietly dropped on arrival. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of cattle lowing and of a wounded animal's noise. It is not the word for a composed prayer; it names the sound made when composure is gone.

A verb of removing a covering rather than of curing. The harm is treated as something laid over a person and taken off, which makes relief an act performed on them rather than a change in the situation.
An imperative that is not a permission. The same root runs through the Quran for temporary provision, and here the command is a way of leaving people to a course whose end the next clause withholds.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sea travel to Abyssinia and the Yemen was the most frightening thing most Meccans did. Ships were small, crews prayed aloud in storms, and men made vows at the rail that they told stories about afterwards. On land the equivalent was a caravan caught without water. Everyone in the audience had heard someone swear an oath in fear and had watched, weeks later, as it quietly went unmentioned.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for the cry in distress appears only a handful of times in the Quran and always in this setting, of people calling out under pressure. It belongs to animal sound rather than to speech. Choosing it means the passage is not describing insincere prayer; it is describing prayer that is entirely sincere and entirely temporary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a claim about human nature that is unusually generous and unusually severe at once. Generous, because it grants that the cry in distress was real and directed rightly, which means the knowledge of God is already there. Severe, because it shows how quickly relief erases it. What is exposed is not disbelief but a memory that works only under pressure, and that is a harder thing to correct.

crossReferences.why: The same pattern at sea: sincere calling in the storm, association again on dry land.
Extends the scene, adding the promises made during the storm and broken after it.
Describes a man calling on his Lord in affliction and forgetting what he called for.

studies.applyIt: Think back to the last time you were genuinely frightened and prayed. Try to recall what you promised, in words or half-words. Most people cannot. Write down one thing you would want to have promised, and do it this week, now that nothing is wrong. The passage is not really about the cry. It is about the fortnight afterwards.

studies.title: Three Commanded, Three Forbidden
studies.meaning: Six things in one sentence, arranged as three and three. Justice is giving what is owed; the second term goes beyond it, meaning to do what is excellent whether or not it is due; the third narrows to relatives specifically, so kindness begins where it is hardest to sustain. Against these stand gross indecency, what is commonly recognised as wrong, and overreach against others. The sentence closes not with a threat but with the word for counsel.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of a surah that has spent its length on blessings, argument and the conduct of communities. The classical sources report no occasion for the ayah itself, though they preserve accounts of its effect on hearers, including a well-known report of a Meccan opponent moved by it. It sits immediately before instructions about keeping covenants and oaths, which gives the general statement an immediate application.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to make two things equal in weight. It is the balance point rather than generosity, which is why the next word is needed to carry the sentence past mere fairness.
From the root for beauty and goodness. It covers both doing a thing well and doing well by someone, and it names a surplus above what justice requires rather than a softening of it.
The root means to seek or desire, and in this form it names wanting past your share at someone else's cost. It is the social form of the arrogance the surah has already been describing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no court and no police. Disputes were settled by clan pressure, arbitration by a respected figure, and the threat of feud, which meant a strong family could take more than its share and a weak one had little recourse. Obligations to relatives were the strongest social bond there was, and also the most easily exploited. Naming justice, excellence and kinship in one line addressed exactly where that system broke.
studies.didYouKnow: A companion of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is reported to have called this the most comprehensive verse in the Quran for good and evil. In many places it is recited from the pulpit at the close of the Friday address, a custom that goes back centuries. The ayah names six things and not one of them concerns ritual.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah presents ethics as something commanded rather than deduced, and then declines to argue for it. What it establishes is that the moral content of revelation is not a separate department from belief: the same voice that has spent the surah describing rain and cattle now describes conduct, in the same register. The final word matters too. Instruction is given as counsel aimed at remembering, which assumes the hearer already knows.

crossReferences.why: Takes justice to its hardest case, standing for it against yourself and your own family.
Warns that hatred of a people must not push you off fairness towards them.
Names the same claim of the relative, set beside the poor and the traveller.

studies.applyIt: Take the third item on the list, the relative. Pick the family member you have the least warmth for and give them something this week that justice does not require: a call with no agenda, a small errand, an unprompted piece of praise. The ayah puts kinship next to justice for a reason. It is where being merely fair stops being enough.

studies.title: What Runs Out And What Stays
studies.meaning: A comparison stated as plainly as Arabic allows, with no image and no argument. What is in your possession is described by a verb of exhaustion, the emptying of a well or a purse. What is with God is described by a participle of remaining. Then a promise is attached, and its terms are unexpected: the patient are repaid according to the best of what they did, not the average and not the worst.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah closes a passage about oaths and covenants, where the temptation named is exchanging an agreement with God for a small price. The commentators read this as addressing people under pressure to renounce their faith for money, protection or standing, which was a live situation in Mecca. No particular occasion is reported. The preceding ayah has already said that what is with God is better, and this one says why.

keyTerms.note: A verb used of supplies that finish and of a well that gives no more. It says nothing about how much there was, only that the quantity is of a kind that ends.
An active participle from the root behind one of the divine names, the Everlasting. Using it of what is with God ties the durability of the reward to the durability of the one holding it.
A superlative, not a general word for good. The reckoning is described as taking the highest point of a person's record as the rate for the whole of it, which is a specific and unusual arrangement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in that economy was perishable in obvious ways. Grain went to weevils, dates fermented, camels died of thirst or were driven off in a raid, and a merchant's whole capital could be one caravan crossing hostile country. Nobody had to be persuaded that possessions run out; they watched it happen. What the ayah adds is a second column in the same ledger, held somewhere the raiders cannot reach.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing clause of this ayah is repeated almost word for word at the end of the next one, which promises a good life to whoever acts rightly. Repeating an ending across two consecutive ayat binds them into a pair, so the reward for patience and the reward for righteous work are given identical terms. The device appears elsewhere in the Quran but rarely this tightly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets up a comparison between two holdings and then, instead of naming what the lasting one contains, names who receives it. That is a deliberate withholding: the reward is defined by its permanence and by its rate, not by its content. And the rate is mercy expressed as arithmetic. Being repaid at the level of your best moments rather than your typical ones says something about how the accounting is intended to come out.

crossReferences.why: States the same contrast, adding that what is with God is better and more lasting.
Everything on earth passes away, and only the face of your Lord remains.
Calls wealth and children the ornament of this life and lasting deeds the better hope.

studies.applyIt: Look at your bank balance and then at your calendar for this week. One of those runs out and one of them is where the other column gets filled. Find twenty minutes in the calendar you were going to spend on nothing much, and give it to something that will still matter in ten years. A person, usually, rather than a project.

studies.title: The Promise Of A Good Life
studies.meaning: The condition is stated three ways and each one is doing work. Righteous action is required, male or female is specified so that no one is admitted by category, and belief is named as the accompanying state rather than as a separate act. What is promised is a good life, and the commentators differ on where it is located: some read it of this world, as contentment, sufficiency and lawful provision; others of the grave or the hereafter. Most allow both.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing movement of the surah, among instructions about oaths, covenants and how to bear pressure. The audience included women who had accepted the message against their households and men who had lost trade and protection for it. Stating the promise for male and female in the same clause was not abstract in that setting. The classical sources report no specific occasion for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: The adjective means wholesome, clean and pleasant, the same word used of good soil and good speech. It describes the quality of a life rather than its length or its comfort, which is why the commentators could locate it in either world.

The verb is to give life, not to grant or provide. Coupled with an oath particle and an emphatic ending, it reads as a guarantee, and it implies the good life is something conferred rather than achieved.

From a root meaning to be fit, whole and in good repair, used of a mended tool or a reconciled quarrel. Righteous action in Arabic is action that repairs something, which is a more concrete idea than being good.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman's standing in that society came through her father, her husband and her sons, and her religious life was largely her household's. A slave's was his owner's. So a sentence that assigns the same promise to male and female on the same terms cut across the ordinary way merit was assigned. Some of the earliest believers were women and slaves, and the sentence would have been heard by them first.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of male and female in a promise of reward occurs several times in the Quran, and in each case the wording is symmetrical rather than additive: the same condition, the same recompense, no separate clause. Here the ayah also switches from singular to plural halfway through, moving from him to them, which widens the promise from the individual to the group.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are being fixed. The first is that the standing of a human being before God does not run through sex, lineage or social position, since the qualifying terms are action and belief and nothing else. The second is quieter: the reward begins with a life rather than a place. Whatever the good life is, it is described as something God gives now, in the same sentence as the reward that comes later.

crossReferences.why: Lists ten qualities twice over, once for men and once for women, in the same terms.
Whoever does good, male or female, and is a believer, enters the garden.
Names the opposite condition, a life made narrow by turning from the reminder.

studies.applyIt: Pick one action today that repairs rather than adds. Fix the drawer that sticks, answer the message you have been avoiding, apologise for a small thing nobody else remembers. The word this ayah uses for righteous action is built on the idea of putting something back in working order, and it is easier to start there than with anything grander.

studies.title: The Better Way To Argue
studies.meaning: Three modes are named and ranked by situation, not by preference. Wisdom is the argument that fits the person in front of you; good exhortation is the appeal that moves someone already willing; and for those who push back, dispute in the way that is best. The last clause removes the incentive that usually distorts an argument, by placing knowledge of who is astray and who is guided outside the speaker entirely.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the final passage of the surah, immediately after a reference to the religion of Abraham and immediately before instructions on responding to injury. The commentators generally read the sequence as a single unit about how a small and pressured community should conduct itself. Some report that the ayat that follow were revealed in connection with a specific loss at Uhud, though the sources differ, and the surah is otherwise Meccan.

keyTerms.note: The root also gives the word for a bridle. Wisdom in Arabic is the faculty that restrains and steers, so it names the judgement about what to say and when, not a body of knowledge.

Speech that appeals to the heart rather than to the intellect, usually with a reminder of consequence. The qualifier attached to it here matters: it must be the beautiful kind, which rules out shaming.

A superlative, so the instruction is not to argue acceptably but to argue in the very best available manner. The same form appears in the two ayat about reward a little earlier, tying the surah's close together.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public argument was a competitive art in Arabia, closer to a contest than to a conversation. Tribes kept orators and poets who fought on their behalf with satire and boast, and a defeat in that arena was a real loss of standing. To be told to argue in the best manner, in a culture where the point of arguing was to humiliate, was to be asked to give up the usual prize.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah does not say what to argue. Every one of its terms concerns manner: with wisdom, with good exhortation, in the best way. The only content it supplies is the destination, the way of your Lord. Commentators reading it as a template for calling others to faith have noted that it spends all its words on the caller and almost none on the message.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause does theological work that is easy to miss. By reserving to God the knowledge of who has strayed and who is guided, it takes the outcome of the conversation out of the speaker's hands, which is what makes gentleness sustainable. A person who believes he can tell who is beyond reach will eventually stop being careful with them. The ayah removes that certainty, and with it the licence it grants.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same instruction to argument with the People of the Book.
Moses and Aaron are sent to Pharaoh and told to speak to him gently.
Attributes the gathering of people to gentleness, and warns what harshness would have done.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone disagrees with you about something that matters, try one thing: state their position back to them until they agree you have it right, before you say anything of your own. It usually takes two attempts. It also removes most of the reason the conversation was going to go badly, which is the whole point of the instruction here.

studies.title: Your Patience Is From God
studies.meaning: Three restraints and then a reassurance. The instruction to be patient is immediately qualified by a clause that removes any credit for it: patience is only by God, which the commentators read as saying the capacity itself is given. Then grief over the opponents is forbidden, and so is the tightening in the chest that their scheming produces. The final ayah answers all three at once by stating where God is.
studies.historicalContext: These are the last two ayat of a Meccan surah, and they close it on instruction rather than on argument. The passage before them permits an exactly proportionate response to injury and then says patience is better, so this is the second half of that thought. Some classical reports connect the sequence to grief after Uhud, though the sources differ and the surah is otherwise placed in the Meccan period.

keyTerms.note: The noun is attached to the hearer and then immediately reassigned. The root means to bind or confine, so patience is holding yourself in place, and the ayah says even the grip is supplied.

A physical word for narrowness, used of a road or a room. Applied to a person it names the squeezed feeling in the chest under pressure, which is being addressed as a bodily state rather than a moral failing.
From the same root as the word for beauty and for doing well by others. Placed at the very end of the surah, it names the second group God is with, alongside those who are mindful.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scheming in that world was concrete and legal. A clan could withdraw protection, boycott a family's trade, refuse marriages, or block access to the wells and the market. None of it required violence, and none of it could be answered by force. Believers in Mecca lived under exactly that kind of pressure for years, which is why the ayah names the physical symptom rather than the injury.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah's last word names those who do good, and its first movement opened with God's command arriving. Between them the chapter has run through creation, cattle, bees, honey, trade, oaths and argument. Ending a hundred and twenty-eight ayat on a two-part statement of where God is, with no further instruction, gives the chapter an unusually quiet close.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The clause about patience changes what the virtue is. If the capacity to endure is itself given, then endurance is not a resource a person spends down and runs out of, and asking for more of it is the natural response to finding you have none. That reframes exhaustion as a reason to turn towards God rather than evidence of failing Him. The closing statement then offers presence rather than rescue.

crossReferences.why: Names patience and prayer together and gives the same assurance that God is with the patient.
Addresses the same tightness in the chest and answers it with praise and prostration.
The assurance of God's company spoken in the cave at the hardest moment.

studies.applyIt: When your chest tightens next about something someone is doing to you, do not try to talk yourself out of the feeling. Say instead, simply, that you are asking for the patience rather than producing it. Then put the phone down for ten minutes. This ayah treats the constriction as real and locates the supply outside you, which is worth testing.
